title: Buy the field (Jeremiah 32)
hookLine: as Jerusalem falls, Jeremiah buys a field as a sign that people will return
carry: plant the tree, sign the lease
last: A LINE NO EXILE CAN CARRY OFF.

cards: The army of Babylon is camped around Jerusalem. Jeremiah is locked in the court of the prison, because the king doesn't like what he keeps saying: that the city will fall.

Then his cousin Hanamel shows up with a business offer. He has a field back home in Anathoth, the family land, and by the law of the family, Jeremiah has the right to redeem it. Buy my field, he says.
The land is about to be in enemy hands. The seller knows it. The buyer is in jail.

teach.b: Jeremiah does the whole deal properly. He weighs out the silver, seventeen shekels, the text says. He signs the deed, seals it, calls witnesses.

teach.h: TWO COPIES IN AN EARTHEN JAR.
teach.b: There are two copies, one sealed and one left open. He hands them to his scribe, Baruch, in front of everyone in the prison court, and tells him to put both in an earthen jar, so they will last a long time. Why the fuss?
Because this isn't really a purchase. It's a sign.
In the King James words: "Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land." People will buy and sell here again. Life will come back.
And here is the human part. Right after the deal, Jeremiah prays, and admits that the siege mounds are already at the walls. He did the right thing, and he still seems unsure.

teach.h: IS ANY THING TOO HARD FOR ME?
teach.b: The answer comes back as a question: "Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh: is there any thing too hard for me?" Then the promise is repeated, almost word for word: fields shall be bought in this land.
Notice the order. The hope isn't a feeling first and an action after.

teach.h: PAY FIRST, WHILE THE CITY IS BESIEGED.
teach.b: Jeremiah pays first, while the city is still under siege. A hope that costs something, gets written down, and gets sealed in a jar for later.
Some readers take it as a picture of a hopeful act when nothing around it looks hopeful: plant the tree, sign the lease, put the deed in the jar.

how: Jews read Jeremiah 32:6–27 as the haftarah for the Torah portion Behar, which sets out the law of redeeming family land, and the purchase at Anathoth is often taught as a picture of acting on hope during disaster.

games.q: you're Jeremiah, in prison, and the city is about to fall. your cousin offers you the family field. what do you do?
o: say no: the land is lost anyway.
buy it, with witnesses and a sealed deed.
promise to buy it after the war.
games.why: he buys it at once, weighs the silver, seals the deed, and has it stored in a jar: a sign that fields will be bought in this land again.

practice: Bring to mind something that seems unlikely right now, a friendship that cooled, a plan you shelved, something in your life that looks besieged, and ask what one small down payment on it would look like: a message, a seed in a pot, a date on the calendar.
Let one answer come, and hold it the way Jeremiah held the deed before he handed it to Baruch. If you pray, you can bring that hope before God.

wordCard.voice: Anathoth, Jeremiah's family land, which he bought from prison as a sign that Babylon's siege wouldn't be the end. Today's word.
